continuity_registry.light: cold rim-light from upper-left; ink-black ground #0B0E14 everywhere. No warm/golden light anywhere — this channel is the inverse of The Engineering Atlas.
continuity_registry.palette: ground #0B0E14 · surface #161B26 · line #2A3240 · text #E8E6E1 · label #8B94A7 · accent electric blue #4DA3FF (per-video domain accent)

accuracy.cooling_tower_plume: CONDENSING WATER VAPOUR only — bright white/pale blue, soft-edged. Never smoke, soot, exhaust, storm cloud, or lightning. A fission plant burns nothing.
accuracy.power_flow: steady glowing conductors and cable runs. NEVER lightning bolts or electrical arcing. Do not use the word 'arcs' in any prompt — it renders as lightning.
accuracy.three_mile_island: TWO towers. Unit 2 = the 1979 meltdown; Unit 1 = the undamaged twin being restarted. Never depict the melted unit restarting.

sides.query_flow: LEFT-to-RIGHT. The human/question side is always LEFT; the machine/infrastructure side is always RIGHT. This matches the shipped thumbnail (phone lower-left, machine right) — packaging and video share one axis.
sides.power_flow: RIGHT-to-LEFT. Electricity travels from generation (right) back through the grid to the datacenter and finally the phone (left). Demand goes right; power comes back left. Never cross these.
sides.scale_ladder: Every rung UP the dazzle ladder (rack -> plant -> fab -> nation -> reactor) is a PULL-BACK, never a push-in. Pushing in means 'look closer at this'; pulling back means 'it is bigger than you thought'.
sides.training_vs_running: training = LEFT bar, running/inference = RIGHT bar (scenes 52-53)

continuity_registry.maps: north up; terrain in graphite #2A3240, unlit; the active region carries accent #4DA3FF and nothing else does

scenes.narration_segment: That took about a second, and it felt like nothing — because it very nearly was nothing.
scenes.purpose: the hook: the weightlessness the whole video will dismantle
scenes._note: the phone in the dark, screen-lit. Cold open on the smallest object in the video

scenes.narration_segment: That answer cost around a third of a watt-hour of electricity and a mouthful of water. Less than running your microwave for two seconds.
scenes.purpose: plant the honest small number so the payoff can't be called a cheat
scenes._note: 0.3 Wh vs a microwave — the honest number, stated before the escalation

scenes.narration_segment: So here is the strange question this video is going to answer. If one AI answer costs almost nothing —
scenes.purpose: state the contract: a question the viewer now wants answered
scenes._note: HARD CUT to the datacenter. The scale-shock the whole cold open exists to deliver

scenes.narration_segment: why did answering enough of them lead one of the largest companies on Earth to restart a nuclear reactor?
scenes.purpose: the tease — name the reactor without explaining it
scenes._note: the reactor teased at distance, silhouette only — the climax is not spent here

scenes.narration_segment: Right now, somewhere, it's late, and someone can't sleep, and they ask a machine a question they'd be embarrassed to ask a person.
scenes.purpose: make it human and specific before it becomes industrial
scenes._note: city at 11pm, push into one lit window

scenes.narration_segment: Somewhere else a student pastes in an essay. A coder asks why their code won't run. A kid asks how big a blue whale really is.
scenes.purpose: breadth — this is everyone, not a niche
scenes._note: the montage of askers — student, coder, kid

scenes.narration_segment: None of them are thinking about electricity. Why would they? The whole promise of this technology is that it feels free, and instant, and weightless
scenes.purpose: name the illusion explicitly — the thesis in one word: weightless
scenes._note: close on a screen: the illusion named — free, instant, weightless

scenes.narration_segment: — a genie that costs you nothing but the typing. And for any one of them, that's very nearly true.
scenes.purpose: concede the honest point up front — earns trust for the escalation
scenes._note: the genie that costs nothing but typing — concede the honest point

scenes.narration_segment: But there is no such thing as one. Right now this is happening about a billion times a day —
scenes.purpose: the pivot: singular to fleet. The whole argument turns here
scenes._note: THE PIVOT: sparks multiply to a billion a day. Singular becomes fleet

scenes.narration_segment: and every one of those weightless little questions reaches back, through a wire, to something enormous, and physical, and hidden,
scenes.purpose: the wire — introduce the through-line the video literally follows
scenes._note: the wire traced back as a schematic line — introduces the through-line

scenes.narration_segment: that somebody had to build, and power, and feed. So let's follow a single question all the way back — and see what it's actually standing on.
scenes.purpose: state the method: we follow one query backwards
scenes._note: transmission lines converging on one blazing datacenter

scenes.purpose: title card — Why AI Is So Expensive to Run
scenes._note: TITLE STING — wordmark + Why AI Is So Expensive to Run

scenes.narration_segment: Let's start with the small number, because it's real, and it matters. A short, ordinary question to a chatbot uses only about 0.3 watt-hours of electricity —
scenes.purpose: deliver the hero small number cleanly and without spin
scenes._note: query travels phone -> server; 0.3 Wh appears small

scenes.narration_segment: what a good LED bulb burns in a couple of minutes. You may have heard that each query gulps ten times a Google search.
scenes.purpose: anchor 0.3 Wh to a body-scale referent, then raise the myth
scenes._note: an LED bulb — anchor 0.3 Wh to something in the room

scenes.narration_segment: That figure came from 2023, on older hardware — and it's roughly ten times too high for a typical question today. The engineers got fast.
scenes.purpose: correct the myth generously — credit the engineers, no scolding
scenes._note: the 2023 myth corrected — generously, crediting the engineers

scenes.narration_segment: Ask it to read a long document, and that climbs to a few watt-hours. Switch on one of the new reasoning models that thinks before it answers,
scenes.purpose: show the number is a floor, not a ceiling
scenes._note: the number climbing 0.3 -> 2.5 -> 40

scenes.narration_segment: and a single hard question can burn forty watt-hours or more — over a hundred times the simple case.
scenes.purpose: the 100x spread — the first real jolt
scenes._note: SHOT-2 re-establish after 2 abstracts. The 100x spread at human scale

scenes.narration_segment: So hold onto the friendly number — 0.3. Not because it's wrong, but because the story was never that one query is expensive.
scenes.purpose: re-frame: the thesis is not per-query guilt
scenes._note: hold onto 0.3 — the reset before the ladder starts

scenes.narration_segment: The story is what it takes to answer a billion of them a day, forever — and to keep making the machine hungrier. Follow the wire.
scenes.purpose: hand off to the ladder — 'follow the wire' is the spine cue
scenes._note: 'follow the wire' — the spine cue, the ladder begins

scenes.narration_segment: Your question doesn't land on 'a computer.' It lands here — in a building the size of several football fields, full of machines that never sleep.
scenes.purpose: first scale-shock: the query's destination is a building
scenes._note: LADDER RUNG 1: the datacenter building, football fields

scenes.narration_segment: The thing actually answering you is a chip like this — an H100. One of them, flat out, draws about 700 watts —
scenes.purpose: hero the chip — the physical object doing the thinking
scenes._note: HERO SHOT: the H100 lifted out and lit like a jewel

scenes.narration_segment: a microwave's worth of power, for one chip. But you're not answered by one. They run in trays of eight,
scenes.purpose: one chip is already absurd — and it is never one
scenes._note: a tray of eight

scenes.narration_segment: and one tray pulls around ten kilowatts — the electricity of about five homes — to do arithmetic, fast, in the dark.
scenes.purpose: convert watts into homes — the unit the viewer feels
scenes._note: 10 kW = five homes

scenes.narration_segment: Fill a rack with trays and a hall with racks, and a single building is running the power of a small town.
scenes.purpose: the multiply: rack to hall to town
scenes._note: ★ PULL-BACK 1/3 — rack -> hall -> the power of a small town

scenes.narration_segment: That is the fundamental fact about artificial intelligence that the smooth little chat window is designed to hide: underneath, it is a ferociously hungry machine,
scenes.purpose: name the concealment — the emotional core of the video
scenes._note: the smooth chat window vs the machine it hides. The emotional core

scenes.narration_segment: and what it is hungry for is electricity. And there is a catch built into physics. Everything that much electricity does, it eventually turns into heat —
scenes.purpose: the physics turn that opens the water beat
scenes._note: the physics turn: electricity becomes heat

scenes.narration_segment: and a hall like this would cook itself in minutes if nobody carried the heat away. Which is the second cost, the one nobody sees.
scenes.purpose: set up cost #2 as inevitable, not incidental
scenes._note: the hall's heat shimmer; cooling kicks in

scenes.narration_segment: The cheapest way to move a mountain of heat is water — so a big part of this machine exists just to evaporate it,
scenes.purpose: why water — it is a heat problem, not a thirst problem
scenes._note: LADDER RUNG 2: the cooling towers exhaling vapour

scenes.narration_segment: the way sweat cools you down. At the datacenter itself, one answer evaporates only a few millilitres — a rushed sip.
scenes.purpose: the on-site number, honestly small
scenes._note: the on-site sip — a few millilitres

scenes.narration_segment: But that isn't where most of the water is. Because the electricity had to come from somewhere —
scenes.purpose: the misdirection: the water is upstream, not here
scenes._note: misdirection: the water is upstream, not here

scenes.narration_segment: and most of the world still makes power by boiling water into steam to spin a turbine, in plants that evaporate their own rivers to cool back down.
scenes.purpose: the grid's own water cost — the hidden second boundary
scenes._note: ★ MATCH-CUT 1/3 — datacenter cooling tower plume -> POWER PLANT cooling tower plume. Same shape, bigger scale: the match IS the argument

scenes.narration_segment: So every watt your question borrowed from the grid had already spent a little water, miles away, before it ever reached the building.
scenes.purpose: connect the two boundaries into one chain
scenes._note: every watt already spent water, miles away

scenes.narration_segment: Add them up, and a single answer costs somewhere around fifteen millilitres of water — a real mouthful. The exact figure is genuinely hard to pin down;
scenes.purpose: deliver ~15 mL and immediately flag its uncertainty
scenes._note: the two boundaries add to ~15 mL

scenes.narration_segment: it depends on where the datacenter sits and how it's cooled. But a mouthful is the right order of magnitude —
scenes.purpose: the humility beat — credibility with the expert viewer
scenes._note: THE HUMILITY BEAT — the figure is contested. Credibility with the expert viewer

scenes.narration_segment: and, once again, there is no such thing as one. Now — where does a chip like that even come from?
scenes.purpose: re-arm the fleet refrain and hand off to silicon
scenes._note: hand off to silicon: where does a chip come from?

scenes.narration_segment: Because before that chip ever answered a single question, it was one of the most difficult objects humanity knows how to make.
scenes.purpose: reframe the chip from component to artefact
scenes._note: ★ MATCH-CUT 2/3 — the H100 (scene 21) -> the blank silicon wafer it was carved from. Rewind on the same rectangle

scenes.narration_segment: The features carved onto it are smaller than a virus, printed by firing light at silicon with a machine so complex
scenes.purpose: the precision — awe, not statistics
scenes._note: features smaller than a virus

scenes.narration_segment: that only one company on Earth can build it. Getting from sand to a working AI chip takes hundreds of steps,
scenes.purpose: the ASML fact — a genuine jaw-drop, kept about the machine
scenes._note: the EUV machine, hero-lit — only one company on Earth

scenes.narration_segment: in a factory that has to be cleaner than an operating room and never, ever stops. And a factory like that is a monster of its own.
scenes.purpose: the fab as its own industrial appetite
scenes._note: the cleanroom that never stops

scenes.narration_segment: One leading-edge chip fab runs on the electricity of a small city and the water of a small town —
scenes.purpose: the fab's power AND water in one line — the ladder's 4th rung
scenes._note: LADDER RUNG 3: a city of power AND a town of water

scenes.narration_segment: millions of gallons a day, purified past anything found in nature — just to keep printing silicon. The company that makes most of the world's AI chips
scenes.purpose: make the volume physical
scenes._note: millions of gallons a day

scenes.narration_segment: gets through more power and water in a year than some entire countries. So your chatbot's brain was thirsty, and power-hungry, before it ever had a thought.
scenes.purpose: TSMC vs countries — then the wit line that lands the beat
scenes._note: SHOT-2 re-establish. TSMC vs entire countries

scenes.narration_segment: Expensive to build. Expensive to cool. Expensive to make. Now do the one thing that turns all of this from a curiosity into a crisis — multiply.
scenes.purpose: summarise the three costs and cue the multiply
scenes._note: the three costs summarised — then 'multiply'

scenes.narration_segment: We followed the heat, and the water, and the silicon. Now follow the thing the whole machine actually runs on — electricity —
scenes.purpose: recap the ladder and return to the spine
scenes._note: ★ PULL-BACK 2/3 — LADDER RUNG 4: one datacenter -> a map studded with hundreds

scenes.narration_segment: and ask a simple question: where does a billion queries' worth of it come from? One query is a sip.
scenes.purpose: pose the aggregate question in the viewer's own terms
scenes._note: a billion queries' worth of electricity

scenes.narration_segment: But a billion a day, and climbing — data-centre electricity is growing about fifteen percent a year, more than four times faster than everything else we plug in.
scenes.purpose: growth rate — the number that makes it a trend, not a snapshot
scenes._note: the 15%/yr growth curve climbing

scenes.narration_segment: Here's what that looks like when it lands on a real place. In Ireland, data centres now draw twenty-three percent of the entire country's electricity —
scenes.purpose: Ireland: the abstraction becomes a country
scenes._note: SHOT-2 re-establish. IRELAND lights up — the abstraction becomes a country

scenes.narration_segment: nearly a quarter of a national grid, feeding server halls instead of homes. In a decade it grew more than five hundred percent —
scenes.purpose: make 23% concrete: halls instead of homes
scenes._note: server halls instead of homes; +518% in a decade

scenes.narration_segment: until the country started refusing to connect new ones. And Ireland is just the sharpest edge of it. Today the world's data centres
scenes.purpose: a state had to say no — the first hard consequence
scenes._note: the country starts refusing new connections

scenes.narration_segment: already use more electricity than most countries on Earth. By 2030 they're on track for around three percent of all the power humanity generates —
scenes.purpose: the planetary figure, framed as projection
scenes._note: the 2030 projection: ~3% of all power humanity generates

scenes.narration_segment: and in the United States, they'll soon draw more than making all the country's aluminium, steel, cement, and chemicals — combined.
scenes.purpose: beat heavy industry — the comparison that lands hardest
scenes._note: SHOT-2 re-establish. Beats aluminium+steel+cement+chemicals COMBINED

scenes.narration_segment: And it doesn't slow down, because of a quirk most people never hear. We picture the giant cost as training — building the model once.
scenes.purpose: set up the training-vs-inference inversion
scenes._note: the training bar — what everyone pictures

scenes.narration_segment: But the forever-cost is answering you, a billion times a day — and running the thing has quietly outgrown building it.
scenes.purpose: the inversion: running it beat building it
scenes._note: the inversion: running it has outgrown building it

scenes.narration_segment: Which is how you end up with a company doing something that would have sounded insane ten years ago.
scenes.purpose: the hinge into the climax
scenes._note: SHOT-2 re-establish. The hinge into the climax

scenes.narration_segment: This is Three Mile Island. If the name rings a bell, it should. In 1979, one of its two reactors suffered the worst nuclear accident in American history —
scenes.purpose: the reveal — a name that carries its own dread
scenes._note: ★ THE REVEAL: the twin towers of Three Mile Island, silent, grey sky

scenes.narration_segment: a partial meltdown that helped freeze new nuclear construction in this country for a generation. Its surviving twin ran on quietly until 2019,
scenes.purpose: the history, precisely — Unit 2 melted, Unit 1 survived
scenes._note: TRANS-2 crossfade = time passing, 1979 -> 2019. The only crossfade in the video

scenes.narration_segment: when it was switched off — simply too expensive to keep running. The lights went out. It was over.
scenes.purpose: the death of the plant — the low before the turn
scenes._note: switched off. The lights went out

scenes.narration_segment: Except in 2024, it came back. Not for a city. Not for a region. Microsoft signed a twenty-year deal to buy the entire output
scenes.purpose: the turn — resurrection, and for whom
scenes._note: 2024 — crews, trucks, the plant stirring

scenes.narration_segment: of a restarted Three Mile Island reactor — 835 megawatts, every watt of it — to match the electricity its AI data centres burn.
scenes.purpose: the hero number the thumbnail promised: 835 MW
scenes._note: ★ 835 MEGAWATTS — the hero number the thumbnail promised

scenes.narration_segment: Over a billion dollars, to wake a nuclear reactor from the dead. Eight hundred and thirty-five megawatts is an entire power station —
scenes.purpose: the cost, then convert MW into something human
scenes._note: over a billion dollars; an entire power station

scenes.narration_segment: enough to light three-quarters of a million homes — and its whole output now has one customer, feeding one appetite.
scenes.purpose: 800k homes, re-routed to one customer — the asymmetry made visual
scenes._note: SHOT-2 re-establish. 800,000 homes greying out as the power re-routes

scenes.narration_segment: That is the real answer to the question we opened with. Your one question costs a sip.
scenes.purpose: close the loop opened in scene 3
scenes._note: 'your one question costs a sip' — the callback to scene 2

scenes.narration_segment: But all of them, all the time, growing every year — cost a reactor. That is why AI is so expensive to run. Not the query. The machine behind it.
scenes.purpose: THE title payoff — held on the towers, one continuous move
scenes._note: ★★ THE TITLE PAYOFF. Held on the towers. Stillness, not a move — the strongest choice available

scenes.narration_segment: Here's the thing I keep coming back to. Any one of these questions really is almost nothing. Your own AI use is a rounding error on your life —
scenes.purpose: hand the honest counter-argument to the viewer, unprompted
scenes._note: back to the phone, the haiku still on screen

scenes.narration_segment: the energy of a query is a few seconds of television. That's true, and it's worth saying plainly. But line them up — a billion a day,
scenes.purpose: concede fully, then turn
scenes._note: a query = a few seconds of television. The concession, made fully

scenes.narration_segment: growing every year, all landing on the same few grids and rivers and towns at once — and 'almost nothing,' repeated at that scale, becomes a reactor.
scenes.purpose: the thesis in one sentence — concentration, not per-prompt guilt
scenes._note: the billion sparks resolve into the reactor

scenes.narration_segment: The weight was never in the question. It's in the machine that makes the question feel free. And that's the part I find genuinely remarkable.
scenes.purpose: relocate the weight — and turn to wonder
scenes._note: the machine that makes the question feel free

scenes.narration_segment: We built something so good at hiding its own weight that a civilisation-sized effort — power plants, cooling towers,
scenes.purpose: begin the roll-call of the hidden chain
scenes._note: the roll-call of the hidden chain begins

scenes.narration_segment: a factory cleaner than a hospital, a reactor pulled back from the dead — collapses down to a blinking cursor and a one-second reply.
scenes.purpose: the collapse — civilisation-scale to a cursor
scenes._note: the whole chain held as one schematic

scenes.narration_segment: There's no monument to a datacenter. The most impressive thing about this machine might be that you never have to see it.
scenes.purpose: the house line — echoes 001's 'no monument to a gradient'
scenes._note: 'no monument to a datacenter' — the house line, echoing 001

scenes.narration_segment: It isn't weightless. It never was. It just feels that way — and that feeling might be the most expensive thing we've ever engineered.
scenes.purpose: the emotional peak — the thesis as a closing aphorism
scenes._note: THE EMOTIONAL PEAK: it isn't weightless, it never was

scenes.narration_segment: So the next time it answers you instantly, and it feels free, and weightless, and like magic — remember what 'instant' is standing on.
scenes.purpose: return to the phone — the callback frame
scenes._note: ★ MATCH-CUT 3/3 — the reactor's towers -> the phone screen. Closes the loop opened in scene 1

scenes.narration_segment: A rack that eats like a town. A power plant that drinks for it. A chip that took a small country's worth of power and water to carve.
scenes.purpose: the ladder recited back, one continuous pull
scenes._note: ★ PULL-BACK 3/3 — the final continuous move: phone -> datacenter -> plant -> reactor

scenes.narration_segment: And, at the end of the line, a reactor somebody brought back from the dead to keep the whole thing fed.
scenes.purpose: land the chain on the reactor — final rung
scenes._note: the reactor at the end of the line

scenes.narration_segment: It's the most impressive machine most people will never see — and it is anything but free.
scenes.purpose: the closing line — held
scenes._note: the closing line, held

scenes.narration_segment: The next time it answers in a second, remember what it's standing on. I'll see you in the next one.
scenes.purpose: sign-off
scenes._note: sign-off — first person, personalised at the mic

scenes.purpose: outro card — subscribe + next video, title sting reprise
scenes._note: OUTRO CARD — subscribe + next video, title sting reprise
